enonce_markdown: A beaker of crushed ice at 0 °C is heated steadily on a stove and stirred continuously. While the ice is melting, what does the thermometer reading do?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

During a change of state the temperature stays constant. The heat supplied is the latent heat: it is used to overcome the forces between the particles, not to raise their kinetic energy.

### Solution

The heat from the stove is absorbed as **latent heat of fusion**. It is used to break the bonds that hold the molecules in the solid and does not increase their average kinetic energy, so the temperature of the ice and water mixture stays at **0 °C** until all the ice has melted. Only then does the temperature of the water begin to rise.

**Answer: a.**

choix.texte: It stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted.
It rises steadily at the same rate as before.
It falls below 0 °C because melting takes in heat.
It rises quickly at first, then more slowly.

enonce_markdown: Wet clothes dry on a washing line by evaporation. Which of the following would NOT help the clothes to dry faster?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Evaporation is faster when more molecules can escape from the surface and fewer return: a higher temperature, a larger surface area and moving dry air all help.

### Solution

A higher temperature gives more molecules enough energy to escape. A larger surface area gives more molecules a chance to leave. Moving air carries the vapour away so that fewer molecules return. When the air already holds a lot of water vapour (high humidity), many vapour molecules return to the cloth, so evaporation is **slower**; this is why clothes dry badly in the rainy season.

**Answer: d.**

choix.texte: Raising the temperature of the liquid.
Blowing air across the surface of the liquid.
Spreading the liquid over a larger surface area.
Increasing the amount of water vapour already in the air.

enonce_markdown: A drinks seller in Douala has a 250 g block of ice at 0 °C. How much heat energy is needed to melt all of it to water at 0 °C? (Specific latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The heat needed for a change of state at constant temperature is $Q = mL$, with $m$ in kg and $L$ in $\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.

### Solution

$m = 250\ \mathrm{g} = 0.250\ \mathrm{kg}$.

$Q = mL = 0.250\ \mathrm{kg} \times 3.4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}} = 8.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Using 250 without converting to kg gives $8.5\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{J}$; using the latent heat of vaporization ($2.3\times10^{6}$) gives $5.75\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$; dividing $L$ by the mass instead of multiplying gives $1.36\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{J}$.

**Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown: A 2.3 kW electric heater is used to boil away 0.20 kg of water that is already at 100 °C. Assuming that all the heat from the heater goes into the water, how long does it take? (Specific latent heat of vaporization of water $= 2.3\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$.)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Energy supplied by a heater: $E = Pt$. Energy absorbed to turn a liquid at its boiling point into vapour: $Q = mL$. Equate them and use power in watts.

### Solution

$P = 2.3\ \mathrm{kW} = 2300\ \mathrm{W}$.

$Pt = mL \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{mL}{P} = \dfrac{0.20 \times 2.3\times10^{6}}{2300} = 200\ \mathrm{s}$.

Slips: using the latent heat of fusion gives $\frac{0.20\times3.4\times10^{5}}{2300} \approx 30\ \mathrm{s}$; leaving the power in kW gives $2\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{s}$; and taking 0.20 kg as 0.020 kg gives 20 s.

**Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown:
A cook on a high mountain finds that water boils at a temperature lower than 100 °C and that food takes a very long time to cook in an ordinary open pot.

(i) Explain why the water boils at a lower temperature on the mountain. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Explain why a pressure cooker cooks food more quickly. *[2 marks]*
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The boiling point rises when the external pressure increases and falls when it decreases.

### Solution

(i) The atmospheric pressure on a high mountain is **lower** than at sea level, because there is less air above. The water boils as soon as its vapour pressure equals this lower pressure, so it boils below 100 °C. The water in the pot is then not as hot, so the food cooks slowly.

(ii) A pressure cooker is sealed, so the steam cannot escape and the pressure inside rises above atmospheric pressure. The **boiling point of water is raised** well above 100 °C, so the water and the food are hotter and cook faster.

enonce_markdown: A student drops 0.10 kg of ice at 0 °C into a pan and heats it until it becomes water at 40 °C. How much heat energy must the ice and the water absorb altogether? (Specific latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$; specific heat capacity of water $= 4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; ignore the heat absorbed by the pan.)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

There are two stages: first the ice melts at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $Q_1 = mL$; then the water formed is heated, $Q_2 = mc\Delta\theta$. The total heat is $Q_1 + Q_2$.

### Solution

Stage 1 (melting): $Q_1 = mL = 0.10\times3.4\times10^{5} = 3.4\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Stage 2 (heating): $Q_2 = mc\Delta\theta = 0.10\times4200\times(40-0) = 1.68\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Total: $Q = Q_1 + Q_2 = 3.4\times10^{4} + 1.68\times10^{4} = 5.08\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Slips: leaving out the mass in the heating stage gives $3.4\times10^{4}+1.68\times10^{5} = 2.02\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$; using the latent heat of vaporization gives $2.468\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$; leaving out the mass in the melting stage gives $3.568\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$.

**Answer: a.**
